name: Fraudmaxxing

lead: Fraudmaxxing (also "frauding") is looksmaxxing slang for temporarily improving how a feature looks with products and tricks instead of changing the feature itself. Typical examples are hair-building fibers for a thicker hairline, concealer for under-eye shadows, shoe lifts for height and photo edits for dating profiles.

The payoff is an immediate, reversible improvement in how someone presents. Users on looksmax.org compile "guides" organised by feature (hair, forehead, eyes, nose, lips, jaw, skin) and debate how much is too much, particularly for height.

paras: Practitioners combine cosmetic products (fibers, color sprays, tinted or concealing makeup, brow products), footwear and insoles that add height, and photo-editing apps for online images. One widely shared guide stresses choosing waterproof versions of anything applied to the face or hair so it holds up in rain or sweat. Results are immediate and last only as long as the product or footwear is in use.

The main reported downside is discovery: forum users note that exaggerated height or obviously applied products can be noticed in person, and one thread title describes feeling bad about frauding. Products carry the ordinary risks of cosmetics such as skin irritation. No published research uses the term.

angle.text: Fraudmaxxing improves how a hairline, skin, face or height reads right away, using reversible products and footwear. Practitioners use it for dating profiles and everyday presentation, often alongside longer-term routines.

lead: Fraudmaxxing, or frauding, is a term from looksmaxxing forums for presenting a more attractive appearance through temporary aids: cosmetics, hair-thickening products, height-adding footwear and photo editing. The word "fraud" is used within the community as slang for any such presentation trick, and a user who does it is said to "fraud" a trait.[1][2] Within the wider vocabulary of the scene, it belongs to the non-invasive side often called softmaxxing, which also covers skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness.[3]

The practice helps people look better directly and immediately. Hair fibers and color sprays thicken the look of thinning hair or a hairline, concealer and tinted products even out skin and shadows, and lifts or thick-soled shoes add apparent height.[1][4] Some users treat it as a bridge while they pursue longer-term changes, while others use it as their main approach.

A long looksmax.org guide organises frauding by facial region, and other threads discuss shoes for adding height, stuffing shoes, and the "irl" (in real life) version of the practice.[1][4][5][6] The community also debates it: one thread argues that adding several inches of fake height is counterproductive because the person is exposed when standing next to someone of that real height.[2] No published studies use the term.

paras: Forum guides break frauding down by feature: hair and hairline, forehead, eye area, nose, lips, jaw and jawline, skin and cheekbones.[1] The entry for hair lists building fibers, described by its author as a basic and well-known option that can improve hairline and density, especially on short hair, followed by color concealer sprays.[1]
A recurring rule in that guide is to buy waterproof versions of any product used on the face or hair, since rain or a sweaty gym session would otherwise reveal it.[1]
Height is the most-discussed category. Threads ask about the best shoes for adding height and whether stuffing shoes works, and others cover the in-person version of the practice.[4][5][6]

The community is divided on how far to take it. One poster argues small, invisible increases are reasonable while large ones backfire because the person may stand beside someone who really is that tall.[2]

Looksmaxxing itself grew out of online forums in the 2010s, and the same communities later moved to dedicated sites such as looksmax.org, where frauding threads accumulated over several years.[3] Thread titles on that forum show the word applied to many features, including height, shoulder width, eye colour, skull shape and photographs.[7][8]

Frauding is framed by its supporters as the quick, reversible end of appearance work, set against slower or more invasive methods. One thread title phrases it as "fake it until you make it", and another argues that large amounts of apparent height are easy to add.[8][9]

The mega-thread's hair section lists building fibers first, described by its author as the best-known option and most effective on short hair, followed by colored concealer sprays that tint the scalp. The same guide organises further sections by forehead, eyes, nose, lips, jaw and skin.[1]

Skin-focused guides discuss tinted products and concealers for evening out skin and covering shadows, and brow pencils for sparse brows. Photo-focused frauding uses editing apps for retouching. Users also discuss the in-person version of facial frauding in a long multi-part guide.[6]

Height aids discussed include thick-soled sneakers, shoe lifts, sock lifts and platform boots, with posters generally favouring modest, less visible lifts. Elevator shoes in general are shoes with thickened insoles under the heel that raise the wearer, the lift sitting inside the shoe rather than showing as a heel.[10] Threads compare footwear brands and ask whether stuffing shoes works.[4][5]

The main internal argument is about degree. One poster accepts an invisible inch but objects to people claiming several inches more than they have, saying this can raise others' expectations of height and exposes the user beside someone truly that tall.[2] A separate thread title records a user describing frauding as making him feel bad.[11]
Another recurring remark is that tutorials are plentiful, with one reply saying fraud guides are oversaturated.[1]

Forum participants name being noticed as the main downside, along with the effort of maintaining the look.[2] Thread titles also show some users reporting negative feelings about frauding.[11] Individual products carry normal cosmetic risks such as irritation.

Frauding guides are popular and also seen as common; a reply in one thread says tutorials are oversaturated.[1] The term sits alongside "softmaxxing", the community word for non-surgical appearance improvements.[1]
